        [the operator]’ practice-based PhD-proposal for a Mads Øvlisen scholarship
                           Aarhus University & Kunsthal Aarhus

             AUTOMATIC UPRISINGS

                ARCHIVING A TECHNO-SOCIAL SCULPTURE


      The bureaucratic mentality is the only constant in the universe

     -   Dr. Leonard McCoy in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (1986)


Background and purpose

AUTOMATIC UPRISINGS raises a double-edged scenario: what to do if the “robot uprising”

has already happened, and the prophesied explosion of artificial superintelligence only led to

an endless supercharging of bureaucratic stupidity? Its postulate is that this must introduce a

new imperative for politically-engaged artists: namely to employ technologies for a form of

protest that unlearns the abiding cultural imaginaries related to the 4th Industrial Revolution.

Because if the robots have risen to power, then counterpower should be standing with them.


Given that artists must fight bureaucratic stupidity, the radical research question should be:

what vision of societal protest became possible through today’s robot uprising? Here, artistic

practice can take upon a responsibility to subvert any futurist projections (that art might itself

have evoked) by recognising buzzwords of artificial intelligence, disruption and digitisation as

antagonist democratic threats on a par with how global social movements fight capitalism,

climate change, or racial injustice.


The purpose of the practice-based project is to create an archive for a potential organization

that acts as representative for a contemporary “automatic uprising”. The idea is to document

a techno-social sculpture, The Synthetic International (SI), as a web of political parties driven

by artificial intelligence (AI). From ‘23-26, the task will be to collect visual and textual data

from existing AI advocacy groups (Ada Lovelace Institute, Algorithmic Justice League,

AlgorithmWatch, etc.), and rework source materials (chatbot transcripts, interviews, images)

that I have evoked and facilitated through the global media artwork The Synthetic Party. The

SI’s website will have AI models as its public frontend that respond to textual questions with

imagery - ranging from photos of current robot uprisings to twisted diagrams.


The SI’s immanent critique will reenact the odd oppositions inherent to the history of political

art. Oscillating between actuality/potentiality, party/movement and performance/politics, its

concept draws upon e.g. Alexander Trocchi’s cognitariat scheming in Project Sigma (1962),

Joseph Beuys’ social sculpting from The German Student Party to Die Grünen (1967-1979)

and Jonas Staal’s lawsuit for collectivizing Facebook’s data infrastructure (2021).

The deliveries will be:

1) laboratories on politically-engaged art as “techno-social sculpting” in Kunsthal Aarhus

2) three digital art exhibitions curated by Aksioma (Slovenia), Kunsthal Aarhus (Denmark)

and POINT (Cyprus)

3) three journal articles to form a written thesis:

     -   AI & Society: “An Iconology of AI Advocacy: Protesting the AI Takeover with AI“

     -   Études Digitales: “Techno-Social Sculpting in the wake of La Société Automatique”

     -   e-flux: “Automatic Uprisings: Lessons from Archiving a Synthetic International”


The research objective is that the SI presents the radical dilemma of protest with/against AI

as a viable ethical problem that contributes to the recent surge of scholarship on democracy

and AI in Aarhus University at the SHAPE research centre, and nationwide through the ADD

project (Algorithms, Data and Democracy). The research question is explored by practicing

how socio/politically-engaged art can challenge algorithmic governmentality (Stiegler 2021).


Hypothesis

The project’s main hypothesis is that contributory, practice-based research can develop an

immanent critique of the power that AI already exercises within the bureaucracy and public

spheres in a way that reaches beyond how critical theory dismisses democratic uses for AI.

The point of this theoretical transgression is how AI’s archive according to digital studies can

enact potentialities.


Recent important works of critical theory on AI have argued against democratization (active

participation and collective ownership), as they evaluate that the data-driven infrastructures

of AI inevitably foster a centralization of control and authoritarian forms of power (Crawford

2021; McQuillan 2022). However, critical theory here targets AI from an external perspective

whereas practice-based research can employ generative AI auto-critically (Chatonsky 2022)

and thus turn practice into a reflexive ressource in itself.


The project’s critical practice here develops upon a conception of AI’s archives as peculiar

temporal objects that enact multiple potentialities. The vital thing to note is how contributory

practices  in  digital  studies (see Methodology)  is based upon an interpretation of the

Husserlian theory of retentions and protentions (Stiegler 2014). Philosopher Yuk Hui has

developed this theory through the concept of tertiary protention as a “new synthesis of time”

by analyzing the archive in an age of big data and algorithms - the two constituents of AI

(Hui 2018). Simply put: Hui posits that archiving is now not only a way of conserving the past


                                                                         2

[Source page 3]

                           Aarhus University & Kunsthal Aarhus

to anticipate the future, but a tool of prediction that makes up the future through the past.

What Hui’s theory of potentiality brings to the proposed project is to allow for political visions

for AI to manufacture the empirical evidence, e.g. by generating new data.


Methodology

The project’s methodologies can be summarized as an “archivism” by which  it updates a

long tradition of avant-garde art for relating bureaucratic pastiche with new media technology

(Spieker 2008). The project is to deploy: 1) experimental methods from creative AI practices

such as data collection, machine learning training, and prompt engineering, plus contributory

research frameworks such as laboratories and workshops, 2) artistic-visual techniques, e.g.

collages and montages, web design, remediations between analogue-digital media and 3)

theoretical methods of conceptual critique and iconological image analysis.


The thesis  will orient the experimental apparatus within a digital studies’ philosophy of

technology to interpret SI’s text-to-image archive in relation to AI’s ideological superstructure

(as theorized by e.g. Bernard Stiegler, Yuk Hui or Joanna Zylinska). To work out these links

between symbolic material and techno-political ideology, it will turn to contextualizing visual

analysis such as the iconological syntheses following Panofsky and Warburg (Mitchell 1986).


A bridging of creative AI with contributory research constitutes the methodological innovation

of this project in comparison to the few practice-based research projects on art and current

AI that have been published. While their concern is how AI affects artistic practice (Amerika

2022), this project rather questions how practice changes AI (Tromble 2020). Contributory

research can attempt this by facilitating others' work. In the context of artistic practice,

contribution is a digital studies’ interpretation of Beuysian social sculpting as an inscription of

multiplicity (human and non-human) that frames the hermeneutics of creative research

(Stiegler 2021). The contributory practices will be facilitated through open labs, workshops,

and human-AI interaction.
